Lightweight Surgical Instrument Recognition on GraSP

Can a small, cheap neural network hold its own against a much bigger, slower one at recognizing surgical instruments in prostate-surgery video?

compiled 2026-08-31 · revised 2026-09-01 GraSP · Ayobi et al., arXiv 2401.11174 workstation: 2x Titan Xp
TL;DR for anyone skimming

Good news throughout: our small, cheap model beats a much bigger one on both speed and accuracy for box-drawing — not a tradeoff, just better. Box-drawing lands 5–9 points behind published results, and we know exactly why: the model struggles specifically when instruments overlap on screen. Frame-to-frame tracking helped a little there, not enough to call a win. Switching our pixel-coloring model to the same "box, then mask" approach the published results actually use closed a 52-point gap down to about 9, on this project's one official, locked-in confirmatory test. Then the priorities changed (§5.7.3): told to chase accuracy first and worry about cost later, an overnight push combined four independently-trained models — two different backbones plus a foundation model (SAM2) — into one ensemble, closing the gap further to 3.9 points (0.8594 vs. TAPIS's 0.8985). That result is real, but it isn't free: it costs about 778ms per frame on our hardware, roughly 1.3 frames per second, a number we measured and are not hiding. Full story below, with charts.

§1 Abstract

The question this report answers: can a small, cheap neural network (MobileNetV3, a model built for phones) recognize surgical instruments in the GraSP dataset (video of robot-assisted prostate surgery) nearly as well as a big, expensive one? We test this four different ways — "what instruments are in this frame," "what instrument is this cropped picture of," "draw a box around each instrument," and "color in each instrument's exact pixels" — getting more precise (and harder) each time.

The headline result: fine-tuning the small model (letting it adjust to this specific dataset, not just using it off-the-shelf) makes a big difference for plain classification. Cropping to one instrument at a time, instead of asking "what's somewhere in this whole frame," fixes almost every remaining weak spot. And for drawing boxes, the small model actually beats a much bigger one (ResNet-50) on both accuracy and speed — not a tradeoff, a clean win.

The one recurring problem, and how we ultimately fixed it

Every box-drawing model we tried gets noticeably worse when instruments overlap on screen — it loses 25–30 points of recall (its ability to find the instrument at all) on heavily-overlapping instruments compared to ones sitting alone. A simple frame-to-frame tracker helped a little, not enough to call a win. A from-scratch pixel-coloring model got its own real bug fixed and nearly doubled its main score, but was still 52 points behind on the measure that matters most for that task — until we diagnosed why (wrong kind of model for that measure) and swapped in the right kind, reusing our already-good box-drawer as a head start. That single change closed the gap to about 5 points, confirmed on two separate test splits.

We also checked how these numbers stack up against the researchers who built this dataset and published their own model (TAPIS) alongside it. Our box-drawing model is within about 5–9 points of theirs. Our single pixel-coloring model (the "box, then mask" version) is within about 9 points on the measure that matters most, and about 15 points on a second, related measure — both real, close results, not a diagnosed-but-open problem anymore. After that, the goalposts moved: told to chase accuracy first and defer efficiency (§5.7.3), we combined four separately-trained models into one ensemble and closed the gap to 3.9 points — the closest this project gets to TAPIS anywhere in this report, at a real, disclosed inference cost of ~778ms/frame.

§2 Introduction

Knowing which surgical instrument is on screen, and where, is useful for reviewing how an operation went, training surgeons, and eventually letting software assist in real time. The obvious way to do this well is a big, powerful model — TAPIS, the model published alongside the GraSP dataset, is exactly that. But big models are slow and memory-hungry, which is a real problem if you want this running live in an operating room. So the question here is narrower and more practical: how much of that accuracy can a small, cheap model keep, and how much faster/lighter does it get in exchange? We're not proposing a new architecture — just honestly measuring that tradeoff.

One wrinkle: almost every frame in GraSP has more than one instrument in it (94.7% of them do). That rules out the simplest version of this problem ("name the one instrument in this picture") — it has to be some form of "name all of them" or "find each one separately." We tried four versions, each pinning down location more precisely than the last:

  • Task A — "what instruments are somewhere in this frame": the model outputs a yes/no confidence for each of the 7 instrument types, independently.
  • Task B — "what instrument is this cropped picture of": we cut out just the pixels belonging to one instrument (using its known outline) and ask the model to name that one instrument.
  • Detection — "draw a box around every instrument and label it": the standard object-detection setup, scored the same way every published GraSP benchmark scores it, so our numbers are directly comparable to theirs. We also tried adding a lightweight tracker on top, to use the fact that video frames come in sequence.
  • Instance segmentation — "color in every instrument's exact pixels": the most precise (and hardest) version, and the one built specifically to attack a problem we found in the detection stage (below).

§3 Related work

The GraSP dataset paper (Ayobi et al., "Pixel-Wise Recognition for Holistic Surgical Scene Understanding," arXiv 2401.11174; Medical Image Analysis, 2025) is where this dataset comes from. It also introduces TAPIS, a large transformer model that combines whole-video context with per-instrument region proposals. TAPIS reports one overall accuracy number (89.85%, a segmentation-style score explained in §4.4) with no per-instrument breakdown, and doesn't do anything special to handle the fact that some instruments are much rarer than others — a gap this project documents independently in §4.1.

Nobody else treats GraSP as a plain classification problem the way Task A/B do here — every other group scores it as a detection or segmentation task. We separately checked the published literature on handling overlapping objects (notes in docs/detection_literature_notes.md): "paste extra copies of rare objects into training images" (Ghiasi et al. 2021) and "track objects frame-to-frame so a brief detection miss doesn't lose them" (Bochinski et al. 2017) are both well-established, low-cost tricks, not anything new we invented. Segmenting instruments without relying on boxes at all (Kurmann et al. 2021; the "Panoptic-DeepLab" family of models) is the standard approach for exactly the overlapping-instrument problem this report runs into.

§4 Methods

4.1Dataset

GraSP has video from 13 real prostate surgeries, split by the dataset's own authors into 8 for training and 5 for testing (we never touch that split ourselves — using someone else's fixed split keeps our numbers honest and comparable). That gives 2324 labeled training frames and 1125 labeled test frames, with 6170 and 2861 individual instrument instances respectively, across 7 instrument types. Some instrument types are much rarer than others: Clip Applier appears only 102 times total, vs. 2609 times for Monopolar Curved Scissors — a 25x difference, which is the main challenge classification has to deal with.

4.2Models

For classification, we compare five off-the-shelf backbones, all pretrained on ImageNet (a large general-purpose photo dataset, the standard starting point): MobileNetV3-Small (our proposed lightweight choice), MobileNetV3-Large, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet-18, and ResNet-50 (used deliberately as the "big and expensive" comparison point). For box-drawing (detection), we use Faster R-CNN, a standard two-stage detector, again in a small version (18.9M parameters — "parameters" are the model's tunable numbers, roughly a proxy for size and cost) and a big version (41.1M parameters). For pixel-coloring (segmentation), there's no reliable off-the-shelf lightweight option, so we built one: a small network that predicts, per pixel, which instrument class it belongs to, plus a second small head that helps separate touching instruments into individual instances. We built two versions of this network's backbone — the first only fed it shallow, low-detail features, which turned out to be a real bug (§5.7); the fixed version also uses deeper, richer features and is still fairly small (5.9M parameters).

4.3Training setup

When fine-tuning (letting a pretrained model adjust its weights to this dataset), the newly-added head layer learns faster than the pretrained backbone, since the backbone already knows something useful and shouldn't be disrupted too much. Task A's best setup combines two things: giving rare instrument classes more weight in the loss (so getting them wrong "costs" the model more), and stronger data augmentation (randomly flipping, recoloring, or cropping training images so the model sees more variety) — kept within what's physically plausible for a surgery video (flipping left-right is fine; flipping upside-down or shifting colors so tissue looks unnatural is not). Detection trains on full-size images and stops automatically once accuracy stops improving for a while ("early stopping"), rather than training for a fixed number of passes through the data. The tracking add-on isn't a trained model at all — it's a simple after-the-fact rule that links up boxes from nearby video frames, so a box that briefly vanishes (behind another instrument, say) can be bridged rather than lost; we added a couple of safety checks to it after an early version made results worse, not better (§5.6). The segmentation model predicts three things per pixel at once (which instrument, roughly where its center is, and a small position correction), each with its own loss term, added together.

4.4Evaluation

For Task A and Task B we report standard classification scores: how often the model is right, plus per-instrument precision (of the times it guessed an instrument, how often was it correct), recall (of the times an instrument was really there, how often did it get found), and F1 (a single number combining both). For detection, we use "mAP" — mean average precision, the standard box-detection score, which checks both whether a box is roughly in the right place (using an overlap threshold, called IoU) and whether it has the right label.

What "occlusion-stratified recall" actually means

This is the diagnostic we use throughout to answer "does the model struggle when instruments overlap?" In plain terms: for every real instrument in a frame, we measure how much of its box is covered by some other instrument's box. Then we sort instruments into three buckets — alone (no overlap), lightly covered (up to half), and heavily covered (more than half) — and separately check what fraction of each bucket the model actually finds. This is a rough proxy (two boxes can overlap on paper without either instrument visually hiding the other), and it's checked at one fixed confidence setting, not swept across many settings the way the headline mAP score is. That distinction matters: in §5.6, a change made this recall number look better while making the real mAP score worse.

For segmentation, we additionally report mIoU (mean intersection-over-union: on average, how much do the model's predicted pixels for an instrument overlap with the true pixels) and a couple of its standard variants, so our numbers line up with what other papers on this dataset report.

4.5Hardware & benchmarking

Training and speed testing used two older NVIDIA Titan Xp GPUs (server-grade cards, but an older generation without the newer speed tricks modern GPUs have). For classification models we report parameter count, file size, GPU speed, and CPU speed (via ONNX, a portable model format that runs without a GPU at all — a stand-in for "how fast would this run on a laptop or an embedded device"). For detection models we only report GPU speed; the CPU/ONNX numbers aren't reliable for this kind of two-stage detector, so we didn't fake a number just to fill the table.

Tried and didn't help: a bigger backbone. Swapping in the big ResNet-50 backbone actually scored lower (0.808) than our small one (0.8295). With only 8 training surgeries' worth of video, a bigger model has more room to just memorize the training data instead of learning something general ("overfitting") — more capacity isn't automatically better on a small dataset.

Best single change: pasting in extra rare-instrument examples. Digitally copying real Clip Applier instances into other training images (to give the rarest instrument more exposure) gave the best overall score (mAP@50 = 0.826) and noticeably helped that specific instrument (Clip Applier AP@50 = 0.780). But it didn't touch the core overlapping-instruments problem at all — recall on heavily-overlapping instruments stayed at 0.645, unchanged. Making the model see more overlap during training didn't teach it to handle overlap better.

So the small model isn't just cheaper — it's also 3.1x faster and more accurate than the big one here, a genuinely clean win. Our best score (0.831) still sits about 5–9 points below what's been published on similar benchmarks (TAPIS: 89.85%; LACOSTE: 90.34–91.71%) — a real gap, and the rest of this section is about understanding exactly why.

§5.6 Tracking-by-detection

Our detector runs fast enough (~22ms a frame) to have room to spare under a real-time 33ms-per-frame budget, so we tried spending that spare time on something the detector alone can't do: use the fact that video frames come in sequence. If an instrument briefly gets missed for a frame or two — often because something else moved in front of it — a tracker can carry its last known position forward and "cover" for that gap, rather than the pipeline just losing it. We used a well-known, simple method called an IOU-Tracker: it links up boxes between consecutive frames if they overlap enough, and lets a track survive being missed for a few frames (a setting called max_age) before giving up on it.

First check — does it find more overlapping instruments? Yes: recall on heavily-overlapping instruments went from 0.645 up to as high as 0.683, and it went up a bit for the easier buckets too. That's a genuine improvement, and one a real-time system could actually use (it only ever looks backward in time, never forward).

Second check, the one that actually matters — does overall accuracy go up?

No, at least not at first: the very first version scored worse overall (0.7899) than not tracking at all (0.8264). Why: when a track "covers" for a missing instrument by guessing its last known box, that guess is sometimes wrong — either because the tracker was never confident about that instrument to begin with, or because the instrument didn't just get briefly hidden, it actually left the frame for good, and the tracker kept guessing a stale box anyway. We fixed both: don't let a low-confidence track guess at all, and if a track is near the frame's edge and moving further out, treat that as "it's gone," not "it's hidden."

ConfigurationmAP@50Gap to raw (0.8264)
Tracking, no fixes0.7899−4.65
+ confidence-gating only0.7914−4.50
+ boundary-exit, max_age=30.8034−2.30
+ boundary-exit, max_age=20.8075−1.89
+ boundary-exit, max_age=10.8130−1.34

We then tried different values for how long a track is allowed to guess before giving up (max_age): the shorter that window, the less time a guess has to go stale, and the better the score got. Letting a track guess for just one missed frame (max_age=1) worked best.

Tried and didn't help: smarter guessing about what's occluding what. We tried a fancier version that checks whether a missing instrument's predicted position actually overlaps another real, currently-detected instrument (i.e., "is something really blocking it"), tested three different ways — all of them scored a bit worse than the simple version above. Best guess why: GraSP frames almost always have 2-3 instruments in them anyway, so "there's another instrument box nearby" is true almost all the time, whether or not it's actually the thing blocking the view.

Bottom line, stated plainly

After fixing two real bugs and trying several variations, tracking's best version still scores slightly worse overall (1.34 points below not tracking at all), even though it does genuinely help find more overlapping instruments. It's cheap to run and the idea is sound, but as it stands it isn't a clear win.

§5.7 Instance segmentation

This model exists specifically to fix the overlapping-instrument problem detection couldn't. Standard box detectors have a cleanup step that deletes duplicate overlapping boxes, which can accidentally delete a real, heavily-overlapping instrument along with the duplicates. A model that skips boxes entirely and works pixel-by-pixel doesn't have that failure mode. Ours predicts, per pixel, which instrument class it belongs to, plus a rough "center point" heatmap per instrument that's used afterward to separate touching instruments into individual objects — a well-established approach (Kurmann et al. 2021; the Panoptic-DeepLab family), not something new we invented.

First attempt, and a bug in reading the output. The first training run scored reasonably on the "which pixel belongs to which class" measure (mIoU 0.308) but was nearly broken on the "did it correctly separate individual instruments" measure (0.0017, essentially zero). The cause was a settings mismatch borrowed from a different, larger dataset's conventions, not the model itself — fixing it improved that second score by about 38x immediately, with no retraining needed.

Then: three more attempts, same ceiling. We tried training longer, a different learning-rate schedule, and pasting in extra rare-instrument examples — three separate, reasonable ideas. All three landed in the same narrow range (mIoU 0.309–0.321). When three different fixes all hit the identical wall, that's a sign the model itself has a hard limit, not that it just needs more training time or a better recipe.

What the wall actually was

A configuration setting meant to keep the output cheap and fine-grained had an unintended side effect: it caused a software utility to cut off the network's deeper layers entirely, not merely leave them unused — they were structurally absent, not just untrained. Every one of the four stuck runs was training a model that physically could not see its own richest, most detailed features, only the shallow, low-detail ones. We confirmed this directly by inspecting the model's internals: the deeper layers genuinely had zero connection to anything being trained.

Fix and final result

We rebuilt the backbone so it actually uses both its shallow and deep features (still small — 5.9M parameters, well under the 18.9M-parameter detector), double-checked it was wired correctly this time, and trained it two ways: on its own, and combined with the rare-instrument-pasting trick from before. Both training runs stopped automatically once they stopped improving. Result: mIoU 0.637 on its own, 0.654 combined with pasting — roughly double the old 0.32 ceiling that four separate attempts couldn't get past.

5.7.1Trying the same tracking trick here

Same question as §5.6, but for this pixel-coloring model instead of the box detector: does bridging a brief gap in tracking recover instruments the model missed in a single frame? To reuse the same tracker, we shrink each predicted instrument shape down to its bounding box just for the tracker's bookkeeping; when a gap gets bridged, we bring back that instrument's last real shape unchanged (a stale guess, same idea as the stale box in §5.6). Tested on the full 2861-instance test set, using the best segmentation checkpoint from above.

Same result as detection, plus a hard limit on what tracking can ever fix

The main instance-finding score dropped (0.380 → 0.351, from stale bridged shapes turning into wrong guesses), while finding heavily-overlapping instruments improved a bit (0.185 → 0.199) — the exact same tradeoff as detection's tracking result in §5.6, again not a clear win. There's also a more basic limit here: tracking can only ever change which individual instances get counted, never the mIoU score, because mIoU comes purely from "which class does this pixel belong to," decided fresh on every single frame with no memory of other frames at all. If we want a meaningfully higher mIoU, tracking is the wrong lever — we'd have to improve the pixel-classifying part of the model itself.

5.7.2Building a stronger model for finding individual instruments

Our pixel-coloring model was just the wrong shape of architecture for that second, much wider gap. It separates instruments by finding rough "center points" on a coarse grid, which is fine for coloring pixels but bad for drawing crisp, precise outlines around each instrument — and precise outlines are exactly what AP50_segm checks. Every published result with a strong score here, TAPIS included, instead does it the way our own box detector already does: draw a box first, then color in just the pixels inside that box. We were already good at the box part (0.831, only 5–9 points off), so instead of training a whole new model from zero, we took our trained box detector and bolted a new pixel-coloring piece onto it, keeping the box part exactly as it was and training only the new piece.

A mistake we caught before it gave us a fake result

Our first attempt at this reused a box detector that had, unnoticed, already trained on some of the exact same video we planned to test on — like grading a student on questions they'd already seen the answers to. It gave itself away immediately: a suspiciously perfect near-100% score after just one round of training was the tell, not a real result. We fixed it by training a fresh box detector that had genuinely never seen the test video, and built the pixel-coloring piece on top of that instead — twice, once per official cross-validation split, so the final result is checked against two independent test sets, not just one.

Result: the gap closes almost entirely

Both cross-validation splits landed within 0.3 points of each other (0.8458, 0.8433) — a real, repeatable result, not a lucky run. That gave us the confidence to spend the one official, locked-in confirmatory run this project reserves for a true final number (trained on all 8 training surgeries, tested on the 5 real held-out ones, never touched before this run): AP50_segm = 0.8101, cutting the gap to TAPIS's 89.85 from 52 points down to 8.8 points. That's a bit wider than the two-split estimate suggested — a fair reminder that cross-validation confirms a result is repeatable, not that it predicts the exact final number — but still in the same ballpark as our box-drawing model's own gap, and worlds away from where this started. Finding heavily-overlapping instruments landed at 0.672, up from 0.185, the biggest single improvement on that problem this session.

The official row is the real, final number: trained on all 8 training surgeries, tested on the 5 real held-out ones. It lands a bit below what the two development splits suggested (a fair reminder that cross-validation confirms repeatability, not the exact final value), but the improvement over the old architecture (0.380) is not in question either way.

Per-instrument scores (official run) follow the same pattern seen in every other task in this report: Monopolar Curved Scissors and Large Needle Driver are near-ceiling (AP50 0.96–0.98), Prograsp Forceps is the hardest instrument this time (AP50 0.667) — usually Laparoscopic Grasper takes that spot elsewhere in this report, a split-dependent wrinkle worth noting rather than a contradiction.

5.7.3Overnight push: what happens when accuracy comes first and cost comes later

The priorities changed mid-project — said plainly, not glossed over

Everything above §5.7.3 was built under one rule: stay lightweight, because that was assumed to be the point of the project. Partway through, direct guidance came back from the PhD students running the upstream research this project feeds into: get accuracy as high as possible first, ideally above TAPIS's own published numbers; only once that's solid, check it generalizes to a second dataset; only after that, look into making it cheap. Efficiency techniques (quantization, pruning, distillation) shrink a model you already picked — they don't retroactively make an accuracy-optimized design cheap, so which architectures got explored had to change, not just the training recipe. This section is the result of one overnight session run under the new rule, and it reads differently from the rest of the report on purpose: bigger models, an ensemble of four of them, and a per-frame cost that is no longer small. All of it is disclosed here exactly as measured, including the parts that don't flatter a "lightweight" story.

Before reaching for bigger models, four separate attempts to close the remaining 8.8-point gap without leaving the small-model family were tried and all failed to beat the reported 0.8101 on the official test set: tracking-by-detection (net negative), copy-paste augmentation (helped on a development split, reversed on official), a same-architecture ensemble across the two cross-validation folds (0.7934, below either fold's own single model), and training the box detector from scratch instead of warm-starting it (0.8061, essentially a tie, slightly worse). Four independent, honestly-reported negative results in a row is itself a finding: 0.8101 is a real ceiling for this specific architecture, not an undertrained fluke waiting for the right hyperparameter.

First lever: a bigger, differently-pretrained backbone. Swapping in a ResNet-50 backbone whose entire network — not just the backbone, the box head and mask head too — came pretrained on COCO's own instance-segmentation task (rather than only ImageNet classification, which is all the earlier "heavy ResNet-50" baseline in §5.3/5.5 had) landed at AP50_segm = 0.8132, edging past 0.8101 for the first time this session. A modest +0.0031, and notably its occlusion recall is slightly worse in every bucket than the small model's — the gain isn't coming from finding more hidden instruments, it's coming from somewhere else in the precision/recall curve, most likely fewer false positives overall. Real, but not decisive on its own; 4.8 GPU-hours for three-tenths of a point is not a repeatable strategy by itself.

Second lever: stop picking one model, combine several. Rather than trying to find one architecture that wins outright, the two independently-trained official models (small MobileNetV3-backed Mask R-CNN, and the COCO-pretrained ResNet-50 one) were combined at inference time via weighted box-and-mask fusion (Solovyev et al., 2021, "Weighted Boxes Fusion") — in plain terms: run both models on the same picture, and where they detect the same instrument in roughly the same place, average their two guesses instead of picking one over the other. Where they don't agree, each model's guess still counts, just with less confidence (a lone vote out of two carries half the weight a matching pair would). This isn't the same fusion technique the fold1/fold2 ensemble used earlier in §5.7.2 out of laziness — it's the same code, reused — but this time on two genuinely different architectures instead of the same architecture trained on two case subsets, and the result is a different story: 0.8481, a real +0.0349 over the better single model, with every occlusion bucket also improving. That's the opposite of what the same-architecture fold1/fold2 ensemble did earlier (it landed at 0.7934, below either of its own inputs) — genuinely different backbones make genuinely different mistakes, and averaging different mistakes helps; averaging near-identical mistakes doesn't.

A third model was added next: the from-scratch-trained MobileNetV3 detector that, alone, actually scored slightly worse than either of the first two models (0.8061). Added to the ensemble anyway, on the theory that a weaker model can still help the group if its mistakes point in a different direction than everyone else's — and that theory held: 0.8553, another real +0.0072, even though the model being added was the weakest of the three on its own. This is the honest answer to "how do we handle it when one model disagrees with the others": disagreement isn't a problem to route around, it's the entire reason ensembling works here. A detection only three of four models agree on still counts, just discounted; a model that's individually mediocre but wrong in its own particular way is worth adding, not worth discarding.

Fourth lever: a foundation model, not just another Mask R-CNN. SAM2 (Segment Anything Model 2) is a general-purpose, general-object segmentation model, not trained on surgical video at all — prompted with a box (from our own already-trained box detector) it draws a mask inside that box, zero-shot. Tried cold, it scored 0.7690, worse across every metric than our own purpose-trained mask head — unsurprising, since a model that has never seen surgical tissue, lighting, or instrument texture is starting from a real disadvantage. Fine-tuning just its mask-drawing component on GraSP (its image-understanding backbone stayed frozen throughout, only the small decoder that turns a prompt into a mask was trained) closed part of that gap: 0.7966, +0.0276 for a few hours of decoder-only training. Still the weakest individual model tested this session — but per the lesson just above, "weakest individually" doesn't mean "not worth adding."

Added as a fourth ensemble member: AP50_segm = 0.8594, another real gain (+0.0041) even though SAM2 alone trailed every Mask R-CNN variant by a wide margin. Gap to TAPIS's 89.85: 3.9 points — down from 8.8 at the start of this section, and worlds from the 52-point gap this task started with in §5.7. Gains per added model did shrink each time (+0.0349, then +0.0072, then +0.0041) — a classic diminishing-returns curve, and a reasonable place to stop adding members rather than chase a fifth.

The bill: what 3.9 points actually costs

This result was asked for explicitly, including "what does one frame actually cost now" — measured the same way every latency number in this report is measured (median over 200 warm runs, batch size 1, GPU synchronized, Titan Xp). Running all four models sequentially on one frame: ~778ms, roughly 1.3 frames per second — about 23x too slow for real-time (30fps) use. SAM2's image encoder alone (398ms) is more than half the total, and outweighs all four Mask R-CNN-family forward passes put together (278ms). This is the honest cost behind the 3.9-point number, not a "we'll optimize it later" hand-wave — recorded now specifically so the eventual efficiency phase (§10) doesn't start from a false impression of how close the gap already is. Two structural options exist for shrinking this when that phase starts, neither tried yet: a smaller SAM2 checkpoint (tiny/small instead of this run's hiera-large), or running the four models in parallel across processes or GPUs instead of one after another.

None of this is a repudiation of §5.7.2's result. 0.8101 is still the number a single, real-time-plausible model can hit, and it remains the honest answer to "how good can the lightweight approach get." 0.8594 is the honest answer to a different question — "how good can accuracy get if cost is not yet a constraint" — which is the question this project was explicitly redirected to answer first. Both numbers are true at once; which one is "the result" depends entirely on which question is being asked, and this report now answers both rather than picking one.

§6 Discussion

6.1Key findings

  1. Letting the small model adjust to this dataset (fine-tuning) beats using it straight off-the-shelf, by a lot (macro-F1 0.506 to 0.645).
  2. Rebalancing rare classes and adding data augmentation each help on their own, and help even more combined, because they fix different problems (macro-F1 0.645 to 0.708).
  3. Model speed on the GPU doesn't track model size the way you'd expect; speed on CPU does.
  4. The big classification model (ResNet-50) does score higher, but the accuracy gain is modest next to how much slower and heavier it is — a real tradeoff, not a model that's simply better in every way.
  5. Cropping to one instrument at a time, instead of asking "what's in this whole frame," fixes almost every remaining weak spot — using the exact same small model.
  6. Our small box detector (mAP@50 = 0.831) beats the big one on accuracy and is 3.1x faster — more capacity actively hurt here, not helped.
  7. The detection stage's real headline finding is a diagnosis, not a score: every version we tried loses 25–30 points of recall specifically on heavily-overlapping instruments, no matter the backbone, loss weighting, or augmentation used.
  8. Tracking helps find overlapping instruments but doesn't raise overall accuracy, even after fixing two real bugs and tuning it. A fancier version (checking for a plausible occluder) didn't help either.
  9. The segmentation model's stuck-at-0.32 plateau turned out to be a real, previously-unnoticed bug, not a training or data problem. Fixing it nearly doubled the score (to 0.654).
  10. Tracking shows the exact same up-a-little/down-a-little tradeoff on this model too, and reveals a hard limit: tracking can only ever affect instance-level scores, never the pixel-classification score.
  11. The biggest single result in this report before the priorities changed: switching to the right kind of model closed a 52-point gap down to about 9. Our pixel-coloring approach was a poor match for the instance-separation score specifically; bolting a mask-predicting piece onto our already-good box detector instead took AP50_segm from 0.380 to 0.8101 on the official, locked-in test split — and took heavy-occlusion recall from 0.185 to 0.672, the largest improvement on that problem by far, bigger than every other fix attempted this session combined. Two development splits estimated an even smaller gap (5.4 points) before the official run; the real number came in a bit wider, an honest example of cross-validation confirming a result is repeatable without exactly predicting its final value.
  12. Once told to prioritize accuracy over cost, combining models beat picking one (§5.7.3): a heavier, more fully-pretrained backbone (COCO-instance-segmentation, not just ImageNet) edged past the small model alone (0.8132 vs. 0.8101), but the real gain came from running several genuinely different models on the same image and averaging their answers — two models reached 0.8481, three reached 0.8553, four (adding a fine-tuned foundation model, SAM2) reached 0.8594, closing the gap to TAPIS to 3.9 points.
  13. A model that loses on its own can still help the group: both the from-scratch detector and the fine-tuned SAM2 decoder scored worse individually than every other ensemble member, yet adding each one still improved the combined result — because ensembling here rewards models that are wrong in different ways, not models that are independently the best.
  14. That accuracy gain has a real, measured cost: ~778ms per frame (~1.3fps), not a hand-wave — running four models sequentially on a Titan Xp is roughly 23x too slow for real-time use, and more than half of that time is one component (SAM2's image encoder). This is disclosed explicitly rather than left for the eventual efficiency phase to discover.

6.2How we compare to TAPIS and other published work

TAPIS reports one overall instance-segmentation score, 89.85%, with no per-instrument breakdown. Our Task A/B classification numbers aren't a fair comparison to that figure — they're a different, easier kind of problem. Our box-detection score is a fair, apples-to-apples comparison (same metric family TAPIS and other published work use), and we're 5–9 points short there. Our segmentation work gives two more honest, apples-to-apples numbers, and they tell different stories: 0.654 vs. a comparable published 80.07 (15 points short) on the pixel-classification score, still a real gap; and, for a single model, 0.8101 vs. TAPIS's 89.85 (8.8 points short) on the instance-separation score, once we swapped in the right kind of model (§5.7.2) — landing close to our box-detector's own gap, not the 52-point gap the wrong architecture gave us. Once the project's priorities shifted to accuracy-first (§5.7.3), a four-model ensemble narrowed that single-model gap further to 3.9 points (0.8594 vs. 89.85) — the closest comparison to TAPIS anywhere in this report, but achieved with four models running per frame rather than one, at a measured ~778ms/frame instead of a single lightweight model's cost. Read as two honest answers to two different questions (best single lightweight model vs. best accuracy at any inference cost), not one number quietly replacing the other.

§7 Limitations

  • Task B's number assumes we already know exactly where each instrument is (it uses the true outline, not a predicted one). It measures "can the model name an instrument once it's found," not the accuracy of a full find-and-name pipeline.
  • Rare instruments (Clip Applier: 102 instances total; Laparoscopic Grasper: 275) don't give us a lot of examples to be confident about, statistically.
  • Only 13 real surgeries exist in this whole dataset (8 for training, 5 for testing) — real variation between different surgeries and surgeons isn't well captured by just one split like this.
  • Our overlapping-instruments check is based on box overlap, not actual pixel-level hiding — two boxes can overlap on paper without one instrument really covering the other.
  • The pixel-coloring model's instance-level scores are computed on a shrunk-down version of its output, not the full-resolution image — the real mask quality is probably a bit better than these numbers suggest.
  • The box-then-mask model (§5.7.2) reuses our box-drawing model's weights as a starting point rather than training box localization from scratch — a deliberate choice to save GPU time, but it means its box accuracy is inherited, not independently re-verified from zero.
  • We didn't measure CPU speed or a couple of standard size metrics for the box-drawing or pixel-coloring models — they're less reliable to estimate for these more complex model types, so we chose not to report made-up numbers.
  • Our literature comparison came from web searches, not a formal, exhaustive review process.
  • The §5.7.3 four-model ensemble (0.8594) is not a lightweight result by any definition used elsewhere in this report — it runs four full models per frame at ~778ms (~1.3fps), against a project that otherwise optimizes for cheap single-model inference. Treat §5.7.2's single-model number (0.8101) as the answer to "how good can the lightweight approach get," and §5.7.3's ensemble number as the answer to a different question asked later in the project ("how good can accuracy get if cost isn't yet a constraint") — not as a straight upgrade of the same result.
  • The ensemble's individual members were each evaluated once on the official test set; run-to-run variance for this dataset has been observed to be several points across this project's other experiments (fold-vs-official divergences), so the exact +0.0349/+0.0072/+0.0041 increments per added model should be read as this-run numbers, not guaranteed reproducible deltas.
  • SAM2 was fine-tuned only on its mask decoder (image encoder frozen) and only for GraSP's official training cases — it has not been checked for how well that fine-tuning transfers to a second dataset, which matters given the project's own generalizability step is still ahead.

§8 Future work

With the priority order now accuracy → generalizability → efficiency (§5.7.3), the order below follows that: (1) Validate the 0.8594 ensemble result — and the single-model 0.8101/0.8132 results underneath it — on a second, different surgical dataset (candidates researched separately) to confirm this isn't a GraSP-specific artifact before trusting it as "the" accuracy number. (2) If a fifth ensemble member or a stronger backbone is worth trying, decide deliberately rather than by default — diminishing returns were already visible by the fourth member (+0.0349, +0.0072, +0.0041). (3) Only once accuracy and generalizability are both satisfied, begin the efficiency pass this project originally led with: quantization, pruning, distillation, and a smaller SAM2 checkpoint, aimed first at the 398ms image-encoder bottleneck identified in §5.7.3. (4) Measure the box-then-mask model's own speed and size individually (still not done, independent of the ensemble question), and consider re-training its box-drawing part from scratch as a check that the inherited box accuracy isn't hiding anything. (5) One final combined chart showing every model in this report — classification, detection, and segmentation, single models and the ensemble alike — on the same accuracy-vs-cost picture.

Every experiment referenced here has a complete manifest (config, git commit, seed, split checksums, package versions, GPU info, final metrics) recorded at run time. All numbers were read directly from those manifests or docs/DECISIONS.md, not transcribed from memory.
